lead: A capability is an unforgeable ticket for one object plus the rights to that object. A process holds capabilities in a list and presents one to open a file, print a page, or write memory. The kernel checks the ticket, not a global table. Language-based protection gives the same guarantee in software: a compiler or virtual machine checks types and permissions before code runs. Only a few universities teach this topic. Browsers, phone apps, and Java virtual machines use these ideas.
prereq: You need: 6.3 for the row form and 6.4 for revocation.

sections.h3: A ticket that carries its rights

blocks.text: A capability is a pair (object, rights). The object is a file, printer, or memory segment. The rights are a bit vector, for example read, write, execute and copy. The process holds a capability list. Possession is proof: the kernel compares the object in the ticket with the requested object, then tests the rights bit. No separate access-list lookup. Tagged memory marks capability words so a program cannot forge one with arithmetic. A file name is not a capability: the kernel must still check the name against an access list. A capability is the row form of the access matrix, from 6.3. The copy right lets the holder give a copy to a child. Some systems add an amplify right: the holder may increase the rights when passing on a copy, which plain copy does not allow.

Copying spreads rights. If P passes C2 to a child without the copy right, the kernel must refuse. With the copy right, the child gets an independent capability for F2. Revocation is now hard: the kernel has no record of the child's copy anywhere, so searching P's own list finds nothing. A handle solves this. Each capability points to a shared entry. Revocation clears the entry or bumps a version number. Every holder fails the next check. Cost is one update plus later faults, not a scan of unknown copies. Without a handle, revocation may need a scan of all processes, or it may be impossible. This is the revocation problem from 6.4 in capability form.

Language-based protection moves the check into a compiler or virtual machine. Type safety stops a program from treating an integer as a pointer. A bytecode verifier checks stack types and branch targets before the JVM runs a class. Stack inspection checks every caller: a method gets a right only if all frames on the stack hold it. Java groups classes into a ProtectionDomain by code source and gives each domain a set of Permissions. AccessController walks the call stack and tests every ProtectionDomain on it. If any domain on the stack lacks the permission, the check fails. A doPrivileged block cuts the walk short at that frame. A class from an untrusted site can be given no file-write permission. When it calls file write, the check fails. This is capability-like: code holds a permission object, and possession is proof. The runtime enforces the rule without a kernel call per access.

figure.caption: Process P holds a capability list, selects C2 for file F2 with read-write rights, and opens F2 from the ticket alone; there is no access-list lookup.

spec.title: Using a capability
spec.aria: A process holds a capability list, selects capability C2 for file F2 with read-write rights, and opens the file without a separate global lookup.

examples.question: Process P holds C1 = (F1, read), C2 = (F2, read-write), C3 = (printer, write). A call asks for write on F2. (a) Show the check and count the comparisons. (b) P passes C2 to a child process. What must P hold for that to be legal, and what does revocation now cost?
steps: Entry 1: C1 object F1. F1 ≠ F2, so no match. Comparisons = 1.
Entry 2: C2 object F2. Match. Comparisons = 2.
Test write bit in C2 rights. Read-write contains write, bit = 1. Access allowed.
(b) Copy is legal only if C2 carries the copy right. Child gets independent copy of (F2, read-write).
Revocation needs a handle or back-pointer to find that copy. Without it, the kernel cannot locate the child's copy, so revocation is impossible or costs a scan of all processes.
examples.answer: 2 object comparisons and write bit 1; the copy needs the copy right, and revocation needs a shared handle or back-pointer.
examples.check:
c1=('F1','read')
c2=('F2','read-write')
c3=('printer','write')
req_obj='F2'
req_right='write'
comparisons=0
allowed=0
for cap in (c1,c2,c3):
    comparisons += 1
    if cap[0] == req_obj:
        rights = cap[1].split('-')
        if req_right in rights:
            allowed = 1
        break
print(comparisons)
print(allowed)

traps: A file name is not a capability. The kernel must still check the name against an access list, so a name is not unforgeable.
Possession is proof. A capability is not a user password or a login identity; holding the ticket grants the rights in it.
The copy right is separate from read and write. A process may read F2 but still be unable to pass C2 to a child.
Revocation by deleting one list entry misses copies. Use a handle or back-pointer, or the kernel cannot find every copy.

quiz.q: Define a capability in one sentence.
quiz.a: A pair (object, rights) held by a process, where possession is proof of access.

quiz.q: Why is a file name not a capability?
quiz.a: A name needs an access-list check, so it is not unforgeable; a capability carries its rights with it.

quiz.q: P has C1=(F1,read), C2=(F2,read-write), C3=(printer,write). Request is read on F2. How many comparisons, and is access allowed?
quiz.a: 2 comparisons; read bit is set, so access is allowed.

quiz.q: What happens if P passes C2 to a child and C2 lacks the copy right?
quiz.a: The kernel refuses the copy; the child cannot get an independent capability for F2.

quiz.q: What does a bytecode verifier check?
quiz.a: Stack types and branch targets before the JVM runs the class.

quiz.q: Compare a capability list with an access list.
quiz.a: Capability list is the row form, held by the process, and needs no object lookup. Access list is the column form, checked per file name. Revocation differs: capabilities need handles for copies.

beyond: Not for the exam. Capability ideas appear in seL4, CHERI hardware, WebAssembly sandboxes, and cloud permission tokens. Search for 'capability-based security', 'Java ProtectionDomain', and 'bytecode verification'. The theme is moving the check closer to the object or to the code.
